Why physical culture still matters.

Objects are not meaningful because they are expensive or rare. They matter because of what they allow us to do.

By The Brooklyn Dispatch · August 2026 · 8 min read

Up until recently, I didn't want to be materialistic. I didn't see the point in buying things I could access digitally. Books, films, music: everything was available instantly, cheaply and almost invisibly.

Over time, though, I started to think differently. The value of an object is not simply that you can possess it. It is that possession can change the way you pay attention.

Convenience makes culture easier to consume. It does not always make it easier to remember.

Objects create rituals

A record asks you to choose a side and turn it over. A book waits on a shelf after you finish it. A cinema ticket becomes evidence that you were somewhere, at a particular hour, with other people.

These are small frictions. That is part of their value.

The Dispatch

Why it matters: physical culture can create a deeper relationship with art by turning access into ritual, memory and exchange.

Sharing is part of ownership

By owning an item, you also own the ability to share it. Lending a favorite record to a friend or passing on a book that changed you gives the object another life. The object becomes part of a social history rather than an entry in a cloud library.
